column1: {{c1::Managed Identity}} avoids application-managed API keys for supported Azure AI calls.
column2:
Azure manages the credentials for a managed identity and uses them to obtain access tokens. The application does not need to store an API key for supported identity-based calls. The target service must still grant that identity permission to invoke the model.
Review source

column1: SQL's external REST procedure requires {{c1::HTTPS}} with TLS encryption.
column2:
HTTPS encrypts the connection with TLS, which protects traffic in transit. The procedure does not support plain HTTP endpoints. The service still needs authentication and permissions to decide whether to accept the request.
Review source

column1: For a logical-server object returned by Get-AzSqlServer, Identity.{{c1::PrincipalId}} identifies its system-assigned identity.
column2:
PrincipalId is the directory object ID of the managed identity. Azure role assignments use it to identify who receives access. It is not the same value as the model endpoint URL or the token's audience.
Review source

column1: The {{c1::Cognitive Services OpenAI User}} role permits Azure OpenAI inference without model-deployment management.
column2:
Inference means calling a deployed model to obtain an output. Cognitive Services OpenAI User permits this use without model-deployment management rights. Assigning a broader management role is unnecessary when the caller only needs inference.
Review source

column1: Use {{c1::CREATE DATABASE SCOPED CREDENTIAL}} to create authentication configuration for a SQL REST call.
column2:
This statement creates a credential in the current database for access to an external resource. For REST invocation, its name must be a URL that matches the permitted request scope. It does not create the external service or grant its permissions.
Review source

column1: For an Azure SQL REST credential, IDENTITY = '{{c1::Managed Identity}}' selects managed-identity authentication.
column2:
This IDENTITY string tells SQL to obtain a token through the configured managed identity. It does not create that identity or grant service access. The called service must accept the token and authorize the identity.
Review source

column1: A Managed Identity REST credential's SECRET JSON uses {{c1::resourceid}} to specify the token audience.
column2:
The token audience is the service the token is intended for. resourceid names that service when SQL requests a token. It is not the managed identity's principal ID, despite the word 'id'.
Review source

column1: The SQL REST example requests Azure OpenAI tokens for resourceid {{c1::https://cognitiveservices.azure.com}}.
column2:
https://cognitiveservices.azure.com identifies the target service for the access token. The request URL separately identifies your particular resource and deployment. An audience is therefore not a replacement for the endpoint address.
Review source

column1: A credential name for sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint must be a valid {{c1::URL}}.
column2:
The credential name is a URL that limits where the credential can be used. Its scheme and host must match, and its path must cover the requested path. Do not use a friendly alias or include a query string in the credential name.
Review source

column1: A credential URL for sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint must not contain {{c1::a query string}}.
column2:
The credential name defines the endpoint scope and must not include a query string. Parameters such as api-version belong in the actual request URL. Keep the authentication object's name separate from the complete request address.
Review source

column1: Use {{c1::sys.sp_invoke_external_rest_endpoint}} to invoke an HTTPS endpoint from supported SQL platforms.
column2:
This system procedure sends a request to an HTTPS endpoint from supported SQL platforms. A controlled application procedure can call it with approved destinations and inputs. Merely wrapping the call does not configure all required SQL and service permissions.
Review source

column1: In SQL Server 2025, enable REST invocation through the '{{c1::external rest endpoint enabled}}' server configuration option.
column2:
SQL Server 2025 includes the procedure but disables it by default. This server configuration option enables the feature. Enabling the feature does not grant every database user permission to invoke it.
Review source

column1: The SQL REST procedure's {{c1::@credential}} parameter names the database-scoped credential to use.
column2:
@credential names the existing database-scoped credential. Its URL-based name must cover the request URL under the matching rules. Selecting it does not grant missing permissions on the target service.
Review source

column1: The SQL REST Azure OpenAI embeddings example uses @method = '{{c1::POST}}'.
column2:
POST sends the embedding input in the request body. @url identifies the deployment endpoint, and @payload supplies the JSON input. This describes the embeddings operation rather than every possible REST request.
Review source

column1: Construct an input payload with {{c1::JSON_OBJECT}}('input': @InputText).
column2:
JSON_OBJECT constructs a valid JSON object from the supplied key and value. The literal key is input, and @InputText supplies its value. This avoids manually assembling JSON text around the input.
Review source

column1: Before EXECUTE, store a JSON_OBJECT result in {{c1::a local variable}} and pass that variable to @payload.
column2:
First assign the JSON result to a variable, such as @payload. Then pass @payload to EXECUTE. T-SQL does not accept this inline function call as the stored-procedure argument expression.
Review source

column1: Capture the SQL REST response with @response = @response {{c1::OUTPUT}}.
column2:
Declare a local nvarchar(max) variable and pass it with OUTPUT. For example, @response = @response OUTPUT returns the response document to that variable. The procedure's integer return code is separate from this document.
Review source

column1: For the SQL REST embedding response, use {{c1::JSON_QUERY}}(@response, '$.result.data[0].embedding') to extract the array.
column2:
An embedding is an array of numbers representing content. JSON_QUERY extracts an entire JSON array or object. JSON_VALUE is for one scalar value, so it is not the correct choice for the whole embedding array.
Review source

column1: The first embedding array in SQL's wrapped Azure OpenAI response is at {{c1::$.result.data[0].embedding}}.
column2:
The SQL procedure places the endpoint's response body under result. Inside that body, data is an array and [0] selects its first entry. embedding selects the vector array within that entry.
Review source

column1: In the SQL REST JSON response, {{c1::$.response.status.http.code}} holds the actual HTTP status code.
column2:
The response object contains HTTP metadata, while result contains the endpoint's response body. This path selects the actual HTTP code, such as 200 or 403. Do not log a fixed success code for every call.
Review source

column1: The SQL REST procedure returns 0 when the received HTTP status is in the {{c1::2xx}} range.
column2:
The procedure uses 0 to report a completed HTTP request with a success status in the 200-299 range. It does not replace the real HTTP status with 0. Read the response document when the exact status matters.
Review source

column1: If HTTPS completes with a non-2xx status, the SQL REST procedure returns {{c1::that HTTP status code}}.
column2:
An HTTP 403 response means the server returned a forbidden result. The procedure returns that non-2xx code rather than automatically raising a SQL exception. A failure to make the HTTPS call at all follows the exception path instead.
Review source

column1: Permit the AIFeatureUsers role to call a wrapper with GRANT {{c1::EXECUTE}} ON dbo.GetEmbedding TO AIFeatureUsers;
column2:
This grant permits members of AIFeatureUsers to call the named wrapper procedure. A wrapper is an application procedure that controls an underlying call. Its effective execution context still needs the REST-invocation and credential permissions required by that call.
Review source

column1: Add an existing database user to the AI role with ALTER ROLE AIFeatureUsers {{c1::ADD MEMBER}} [app-service-identity];
column2:
The database user must already exist before ADD MEMBER can add it to the role. The role supplies permissions inside SQL, such as access to a wrapper procedure. It does not assign an Azure role on the model service.
Review source

column1: Direct SQL REST invocation requires the database permission {{c1::EXECUTE ANY EXTERNAL ENDPOINT}}.
column2:
This permission allows direct use of the SQL REST invocation feature. It is broader than EXECUTE on one approved wrapper procedure. Restrict direct grants if applications must use a controlled path to external services.
Review source

column1: Using a credential with SQL REST invocation requires {{c1::REFERENCES}} permission on that database-scoped credential.
column2:
REFERENCES permits use of the named database-scoped credential for the call. It does not itself permit REST invocation or grant service-side access. Those checks are separate layers of the request.
Review source

column1: An Azure Machine Learning managed online endpoint uses auth_mode: {{c1::aad_token}} for Microsoft Entra authentication.
column2:
aad_token requires a Microsoft Entra access token for requests to the managed online endpoint. The token identifies the caller, and Azure permissions determine whether scoring is allowed. Kubernetes online endpoints do not support this mode.
Review source

column1: For Azure Machine Learning online scoring, request a data-plane token for {{c1::https://ml.azure.com/}}.
column2:
Scoring means sending data to a deployed model for inference. Its token targets https://ml.azure.com/, the scoring service. A token for Azure resource management targets a different service and is not interchangeable.
Review source

column1: Use {{c1::SYSUTCDATETIME()}} to record a UTC datetime2 timestamp for an AI call.
column2:
SYSUTCDATETIME() returns the current UTC time as datetime2. UTC provides a common basis for comparing events across environments. Use the same time basis when recording the start and end of a call.
Review source

column1: {{c1::ORIGINAL_LOGIN()}} identifies the login that first established the SQL session.
column2:
ORIGINAL_LOGIN() records the identity that established the SQL connection, even if execution context later changes. With a shared application login, many human users have the same value. Log trusted application-user context separately when individual attribution is required.
Review source

column1: DATEDIFF({{c1::millisecond}}, @StartTime, SYSUTCDATETIME()) measures AI-call duration in milliseconds.
column2:
Set @StartTime to SYSUTCDATETIME() before invoking the service. DATEDIFF with millisecond counts the millisecond boundaries between that value and the current UTC time. It measures the interval, not the endpoint's HTTP status.
Review source

column1: After GROUP BY CallerPrincipal, use {{c1::HAVING}} COUNT(*) > 100 to select groups above 100 AI calls.
column2:
HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY calculates their aggregate values. COUNT(*) > 100 keeps callers with more than 100 matching log records. Use WHERE before grouping to restrict which time period contributes to each count.
Review source

column1: Fabric SQL database can use a {{c1::HTTPEndpointHeaders}} credential for API-key access to an external embedding model.
column2:
HTTPEndpointHeaders sends authentication values from the credential as request headers. An external embedding endpoint can use an api-key header this way. Fabric workspace membership does not automatically supply that external service credential.
Review source

column1: Fabric's prebuilt AI services charge usage against {{c1::Fabric capacity}}.
column2:
The integrated AI requests consume Fabric capacity and appear under the Copilot and AI meter. Spark compute used to run a notebook is reported separately. An AI request is therefore not accounted for only by the notebook's compute usage.
Review source

column1: Inspect Fabric AI-service capacity consumption in the {{c1::Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app}}.
column2:
The Capacity Metrics app shows how workloads consume Fabric capacity. Inspect the Copilot and AI meter for integrated AI-service usage. This helps separate AI consumption from Spark compute charges.
Review source

column1: A tenant administrator must enable the relevant {{c1::tenant setting}} before Copilot can be used in Fabric SQL database.
column2:
A tenant administrator controls the relevant Copilot tenant setting. Membership in a workspace does not replace that approval. Supported paid capacity and regional availability are additional requirements.
Review source
